annotations.keyFindings: In 62 referral dogs, a supervised programme gave 9.4 against 2.1 percent weight loss and improved owner-reported mobility by 6.1 against 1.8 points at 16 weeks.
annotations.limitations: Referral population; owners not blinded; 16 weeks only.

annotations.keyFindings: Only 38 percent of 1,240 dogs in nurse-led clinics attended for six months; completers lost a median 8.1 percent.
annotations.limitations: Outcomes of non-completers unknown; no comparison group.

annotations.keyFindings: The 11-item index is reliable (0.88 over one week); owners judged about 4 points a meaningful change; change scores had a standard deviation of 8.
Owners reported about 2 points of improvement when dogs received an inactive tablet; activity counts correlated 0.41 with owner scores.
Adherence to the food allowance fell from 81 to 57 percent of days over six months; 34 percent of owners reported hunger behaviours.
Across 14 practice-based pragmatic trials, recruitment was a median 3.2 animals per practice per month and central web allocation reduced protocol deviations.
annotations.limitations: Methods summary; trials varied in size and species.

annotations.keyFindings: Dogs losing at least 10 percent of weight more often had anti-inflammatory doses reduced (29 against 8 percent).
annotations.limitations: No protocol for dose changes; owner preference possible.

claims.text: In a referral trial, a supervised weight loss programme improved owner-reported mobility by a mean of 6.1 points against 1.8 points with diet advice alone.
claims.passage: Owner-reported mobility scores improved by a mean of 6.1 points on a 44-point index in the programme group and by 1.8 points with advice alone.
claims.interpretation: An effect near 4 points is plausible in first-opinion practice, where motivation is lower.

claims.text: Owners' judgement of meaningful change on the 11-item mobility index corresponded to about 4 points.
claims.passage: Owners' judgements of meaningful change corresponded to a difference of about 4 points.
claims.interpretation: Sets the smallest difference worth detecting.

claims.text: Owners reported about 2 points of improvement when their dogs received an inactive tablet.
claims.passage: owners still reported improvement of about 2 points
claims.interpretation: Unblinded owner scores need a blinded secondary outcome.

claims.text: Only 38 percent of dogs in nurse-led weight clinics attended for six months.
claims.passage: Only 38 percent of dogs attended for six months.
claims.interpretation: Retention is a key outcome and a threat to follow-up.

claims.text: Pragmatic trials that allocated animals centrally by a web system reported fewer protocol deviations than those using envelopes held in practices.
claims.passage: Trials that allocated animals centrally by a web system reported fewer protocol deviations than those using envelopes held in practices.
claims.interpretation: Use central web allocation stratified by practice.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One referral trial found supervised weight loss improved owner-reported mobility by more than the 4-point change owners consider meaningful, but owners were unblinded and owners report improvement even with an inactive tablet. Nurse-led clinics in first-opinion practice lose most dogs before six months, adherence to food allowances falls over time and hunger behaviours are common. Practice-based pragmatic trials recruit about three animals per practice per month and run more cleanly with central allocation. The evidence supports a pragmatic comparison with a blinded secondary outcome and close attention to retention.
gradeRationale: One small referral trial with unblinded owners and several observational studies; indirect for first-opinion practice and imprecise.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty low.
